2.-design-principles/1.-design-philosoph.title: 1. Design Philosophy
2.-design-principles/1.-design-philosoph.description:
Plagues has exactly three kinds of process and one broker. Once you have this picture, everything else in the wiki is a detail hanging off it.The single most important arrow is the one that isn't there: an app never connects to a worker. That dotted "never" is the whole security model.A worker is a tiny MagicOnion-hosted service that exposes one or more capabilities. A capability is just a static C# method marked with Eclipse's [SeaOfDirac] attribute:[SeaOfDirac("GetAccInfo", new[] { "accountName" }, typeof(PublicAccount), typeof(string))] public static PublicAccount GetAccInfo(string accountName) { /* privileged work */ } At startup a worker: Runs Notary anti-tamper over its own folder (or trusts the Manager's pre-launch check when Manager-managed). Reads the per-worker PSK and the Manager's public identity key, both handed to it out-of-band at launch (never on disk). Binds an ephemeral loopback port and publishes a WorkerAnnouncement (address + capabilities + public Kyber key + pid) so the Manager can find it. Serves the Eclipse protocol — but only completes a handshake for a peer that holds the PSK and presents a valid Manager signature.
See 2 - Creating a Worker.One Manager per machine. It is the only process that: Checksums + launches + supervises every worker, restarting one that dies or trips its tamper guard. Holds the master key (encrypts the permission store), the per-app PSKs, the per-worker PSKs, and its own Dilithium identity keypair. Runs the broker: an Eclipse endpoint apps connect to. On each call it authenticates the app, checks XRUIOS.Permission, relays to the owning worker over a warm pooled session, and re-encrypts the reply.
See 4 - Registering and Launching.An app holds only its own credential and the broker address. It never sees a worker, never holds the master key. It opens one Eclipse session to the Manager and calls capabilities by name:await using var xruios = await EclipseSecureClient.ConnectAsync(brokerAddr, appId, appPsk, identity: appId); var acc = await xruios.InvokeAsync<PublicAccount>("GetAccInfo", new() { ["accountName"] = Environment.UserName });
See 3 - Creating an App.Identity is bound by the tier above — never self-reported. An app's identity is the appId the Manager minted for it. The app can't claim to be another app; the Manager resolves the PSK and checks permissions by that id. A worker's peer is the Manager, proven by the Manager's signature (asymmetric), not merely by holding a shared secret. This is the same discipline HangarBay uses for mods — bind the id, don't trust the claim — applied one tier up. Eclipse's AeadChannel derives separate keys per direction (k_c2s, k_s2c) and gives each an independent AES-256-GCM cipher with a monotonic sequence counter. So a request and its reply are individually encrypted and authenticated, and neither can be replayed or reordered. The broker exploits this: it decrypts the worker's reply on the Manager→worker channel and re-encrypts the exact bytes onto the Manager→app channel, so end-to-end confidentiality holds across both hops without the Manager ever exposing plaintext to a third channel.

2.-design-principles/2.-plague-template..title: 2. Plague Template
2.-design-principles/2.-plague-template..description:
Three dotnet new templates ship in Plagues-Protocol/templates/, so you can assemble a whole
XRUIOS solution from the command line or Visual Studio's New Project / New Item dialogs.dotnet new install ./templates/xruios-manager
dotnet new install ./templates/xruios-worker
dotnet new install ./templates/xruios-app
dotnet new list xruios lists all three. Re-run with --force after editing a template.
Create an empty solution.
dotnet new xruios-manager -n XRUIOS.Manager — the core (checksums, launches, supervises,
holds the master key + per-app PSKs, runs the permission-checked broker).
dotnet new xruios-worker a few times — one per capability, under the solution.
Point the Manager's ResolveWorkers() at those workers, register your apps + grants, run.
Drop xruios-app into whatever UI project talks to the Manager.
dotnet new sln -n "The XRUIOS"
dotnet new xruios-manager -n XRUIOS.Manager && dotnet sln add XRUIOS.Manager
dotnet new xruios-worker -n XRUIOS.WeatherDataHandler --capability GetForecast && dotnet sln add XRUIOS.WeatherDataHandler
dotnet new xruios-worker -n XRUIOS.AccountDataHandler --kind crossplatform && dotnet sln add XRUIOS.AccountDataHandler
"Cross-platform" is not a Windows+Linux pair — it's whether one build branches internally.Both are a single net9.0 binary that runs on Windows and Linux. Parameters: --kind,
--capability (first capability name).The Manager's .csproj references the shared layer and permission store by relative path
(..\..\Plagues-Protocol\XRUIOS.Interfaces, ..\..\XRUIOS.Permission\..., ..\..\Plagues-Protocol\libs\*.dll).
Generate it into a solution folder beside Plagues-Protocol and XRUIOS.Permission (the canonical
GitHub\<solution>\XRUIOS.Manager\ layout), or fix those paths once. It ships with a worked calendar
example in Program.cs — adapt ResolveWorkers() and step [4] for your fleet.xruios-app adds one file (XruiosAppClient.cs) to an existing project — CMD, OpenSilver,
Avalonia, WPF, MAUI. It acquires Manager credentials (env handoff or self-enroll with binary
attestation), opens the Eclipse secure session, and calls capabilities. The host project just needs a
reference to XRUIOS.Interfaces. Parameters: --namespaceName, --capability.await using var xruios = await XruiosAppClient.ConnectAsync("weather");
string forecast = await xruios.CallAsync<string>("GetForecast", new() { ["city"] = "Hollvania" });
Installed dotnet new templates appear in VS. Turn on Tools → Options → Environment → Preview
Features → "Show all .NET templates in the New Project dialog," restart, then:
File → New → Project → search xruios → the Manager and Worker.
Right-click a project → Add → New Item → search xruios → the App Client.

1.welcome/welcome.html.title: Welcome
1.welcome/welcome.html.description:
A fully local, zero-trust runtime that splits every privileged operation into isolated, self-defending agents — so a single breach never conquers the machine.The Plagues Protocol is the ultra-minimalist, zero-trust local RPC substrate that powers every interaction inside XRUIOS (Walker Industries' cross-platform framework / OS / abstraction layer). It pairs Eclipse (post-quantum encrypted app-to-app transport), Notary (code-signing + on-disk anti-tamper), and Pariah Cybersecurity (the PQC primitives + SecureData) into a runtime where nothing trusts anything by default.Windows • Linux • Fully Offline • Post-Quantum Resistant • No BSThe Plagues Protocol enforces a cryptographically-sealed boundary on the same machine between three kinds of process, brokered by a single trusted core. The XRUIOS.Manager is the trusted core. It checksums and launches the workers, holds the master key and every per-app password, and is the only thing that talks to a worker or relays data between apps. Workers (the Plagues part) are tiny, single-purpose services that own one privileged capability each — an account handler, a calendar store, a device bridge. A worker verifies its own on-disk footprint before it serves a byte, and it will only complete a handshake with the Manager. Apps are ordinary programs. They never see a worker and never hold the master key. They ask the Manager, the Manager checks XRUIOS.Permission, and only then does the answer come back. Every hop is an Eclipse channel: mutual authentication with a pre-shared key + an ephemeral Kyber key exchange, then AES-256-GCM with per-message nonces and an HMAC transcript. Injecting a false request or reading a real one from another local process is, by design, not feasible.The Plagues Protocol follows three rules: Never trust the caller — identity is bound by the tier above (the Manager, then the app), never self-reported. Contain, don't just permit — a permission decides what's allowed; the cryptographic boundary makes everything else impossible. A single breach can never conquer the machine — a fully compromised userland app still cannot escalate, cannot reach a worker, and cannot exfiltrate privileged data. "A single breach can never conquer the machine." Everything is a free, open-source Walker Industries library. Plagues consumes them as DLL references — you don't rebuild them into your solution.Target framework: .NET 9 for the Plagues projects; the referenced DLLs target .NET 8 and are consumed cleanly.

info_allowExpand.description: Allow the user to pop-out the graph view to take up the whole screen

info_attractionForce.description: How much should linked nodes attract each other? This will make the graph appear more clustered.

info_linkLength.description: How long should the links between nodes be? The shorter the links the more connected nodes will cluster together.

info_repulsionForce.description: How much should nodes repel each other? This will make disconnected parts more spread out.

info_centralForce.description: How much should nodes be attracted to the center? This will make the graph appear more dense and circular.

info_edgePruning.description: Edges with a length above this threshold will not be rendered, however they will still contribute to the simulation. This can help large tangled graphs look more organised. Hovering over a node will still display these links.

info_minNodeRadius.description: How small should the smallest nodes be? The smaller a node is the less it will attract other nodes.

info_maxNodeRadius.description: How large should the largest nodes be? Nodes are sized by how many links they have. The larger a node is the more it will attract other nodes. This can be used to create a good grouping around the most important nodes.
